w: Zalipie lies in the quiet countryside of Lesser Poland, a small cluster of houses that feels more like a living painting than a village. Since the late 19th century the women here have covered their homes — walls, shutters, gables, even dog kennels and chicken coops — with bright floral patterns, birds, and geometric motifs in vivid colours. The tradition began practically. Homes had no chimneys and interiors grew black with soot. Women made brushes from split birch twigs and painted the walls white with a mixture of lime, milk and egg to brighten the rooms. Over time the white circles became flowers, then whole gardens of painted blooms. The style was passed down through generations, each woman adding her own touch while keeping the village's distinctive look. Today the paintings continue. Some houses are freshly done each spring; others show the gentle fading of older layers. A small museum (Dom Malarek) preserves examples and stories, but the real experience is walking the lanes and seeing the art still alive on working buildings. Stand in the middle of the village on a sunny morning and the colours seem to hum against the green fields.
